As a starter, I thought I'd be useful to provide some opening
remarks about the Authority's Electricity Industry
Participation Code and the Authority.
The Electricity Industry Act sets out the framework for the industry,
for industry governance, and it includes establishing
the Authority as an independent rule-making body, the scope of
its rule-making powers, and the processes the Authority must
follow when making or amending the Electricity Industry
Participation Code, the rules of the electricity industry.
Since it was established in 2010, the
Authority has focused on maintaining existing and making new
rules necessary to operate the largest and most
complex machine in New Zealand.
We're doing this at a time of unprecedented change in the energy
sector, and it's through these rules that we meet our main
objective to promote competition, reliability, and the
efficient operation of the electricity industry for the long-term
benefit of consumers.
More recently, the Authority was given the additional objective of protecting
the interests of domestic and small business consumers in relation
to the supply of electricity.
Mr Miller has made five complaints about different provisions
of the code under various standing orders.
In summary, Mr Miller thinks the code could be better in several
areas. We agree. His complaint is that the code's
inadequacy rises to the level of a
breach of standing orders. We disagree for the reasons we
set out in our written submissions.
The code needs to be kept under review and updated in response to
new and changing technologies and business models.
The Authority is consistently vigilant for opportunities to
amend the code so it better promotes achievement of our main
objective and the interests of consumers.
When the Authority identifies a part of the code that no longer best
promotes those outcomes, we act to amend it in a
transparent and timely manner.
To amend the code, the Authority is generally required to consult
and to assess the costs and benefits of proposed amendments.
Many of the matters Mr Miller complains about are already being considered
through the statutory process updating the code.
Consultations are public, and we would welcome the submissions
from Mr Miller on any of our code amendment proposals.
And we don't make these code changes alone.
To aid the Authority in amending the code, the act requires the
Authority to
establish the Security and Reliability Council and at
least one advisory group. Currently, the Authority
has six industry working groups in operation.
In the last two and a half years, the Authority has made 52
code changes.
And I note that this is more changes than in the previous five
years. The pace of these changes reflects the changing
nature of the industry.
The Authority prioritizes its work based on the
benefits of any amendment relative to others.
This prioritization applies to the issues raised by Mr Miller,
and we have set out in our written submission some of the work the
Authority is currently doing in this area.
While we might have thoughts on the policy positions Mr Miller
advocates for, until we have done work to develop a
policy, including any related code amendments
and consulted on it, we cannot be certain that the policy is the
right one. We consider the regulatory framework and the act
enables the Authority to address the policy issues
raised by Mr Miller's complaint. That's all I have to say
in opening, and we're open to questions from the committee.
For convenience, I will ask my fellow
Authority team members to lead those questions.
I will contribute as necessary. Thank you.
Thank you, Erik. Thank you.

I

Yeah

Yeah

So this narrowed submission goes to grounds A and H of the complaint

Parliament delegated curriculum-making authority to the minister under Section
90 of the Education and Training Act.
Section 4 of the act states its purposes include establishing and
regulating an education system that is high quality, culturally
responsive, seamless, and inclusive, and that honors Te Tiriti of
Waitangi and supports Māori-Crown relationships.
My submission is that a delegated legislative power of this kind is normally
expected, I would say, to be exercised in a way that is transparent and
traceable through the documentary record so that Parliament and this committee
can verify that it's been exercised consistently with that statutory
purpose.
The documentary record, which I know I've sent you a bunch of bits of,
contains a number of curriculum development documents, design principles,
design criteria, consultation records, curriculum development processes,
and then the final curriculum statements.
The curriculum development record includes different curriculum architectures at
different stages. Those include the Understand Know Do,
Themes Knowledge Skills, the UKD Progress Outcomes, and then the
final Strands Knowledge Practice structure that was used in the final document.
The documentary record also shows different treatments of Te Tiriti of Waitangi by
cultural foundations, inclusion and equity across the successive
curriculum development document.
Development record further shows agreed design principles, criteria, writing
groups, quality assurance processes, error review, and other revision
process. My submission is that this documentary pathway connecting these
elements to the final curriculum statements made under Section 90 is not
readily apparent from the record itself.
Mm.
The question I guess I'm posing to the committee is whether the documentary
record demonstrates that this delegated power has been exercised
transparently and in a manner that can be traced through the record.
And that's the standard I'm asking the committee to apply under grounds A and H of
the complaint.
Cool. Okay.
